newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Inflation targets may help smooth running U.S. economy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Inflation targets may help smooth running U.S. economy.

text.p: As the Federal Reserve attempts to keep U.S. growth on track for a seventh year, some experts say a new tool -- inflation targets -- could help with the job of maintaining a smoothly running economy.
A number of economists inside and outside the Fed are touting the benefits of setting specific goals for inflation and using them to guide interest-rate decisions.
The strategy is being used in some other developed countries, such as Canada, Britain and New Zealand and is under consideration by the new European Central Bank.
Proponents like the anti-inflation discipline that the targets impose.
Critics say it takes flexibility away from central banks and may cause monetary authorities to focus on current inflation instead of looking at economic data that can predict the future rate.
Among the most prominent advocates of inflation targets in the United States is New York Fed President William McDonough.
He has suggested the Fed aim for a rate of 0.5 percent to 2.0 percent on the so-called "core" Consumer Price Index (CPI), which excludes volatile food and energy components.
While not entirely a novel concept, inflation targets have come into vogue in the economics profession because they offer an objective measure of a central bank's performance
MONEY SUPPLY TARGETS FALLEN OUT OF FAVOUR

Money supply targets, once key for many central banks, have fallen out of favour over the past decade because distortions have rendered them far less reliable as indicators of economic activity and inflation.

"Targets would be a way for people to have more confidence that the Fed would continue to achieve low inflation," said Allan Meltzer, economics professor at Carnegie Mellon University. "We need to pin the Fed down on a goal and have them make a commitment to achieving it."
Unlike the money supply, inflation data is a lagging indicator -- one reason critics are wary of targets.

"When you are operating monetary policy there are reasonably long lags so that you might not see the impact from a policy move for a year or more," said economist Stephen Cecchetti of Ohio State University. Focusing on current inflation could lead the Fed to react to economic trends that have already changed, he said.
GREENSPAN'S VIEW OF TARGETS DEBATED
Fed chairman Alan Greenspan has not stated a position on the subject and opinions differ on where he stands.
The Fed chief, though, describes price stability as the point where inflation is so minimal that it is no longer a factor in the economic decisions of businesses and households.
Speaking in Belgium this month, he suggested the goal had not been achieved yet but also stressed the difficulty of gauging true inflation given flaws in the CPI.
"Inflation expectations throughout the economy must fall," he said, adding, "We are having increasing difficulty pinning down the notion of what constitutes a stable price level."
Such flaws might be one obstacle to establishing inflation targets in the United States, experts said.

Ralph Bryant, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said that in some sense the Fed already has a target range for inflation but has not formalised it: "They think it's somewhere above zero but not as high as three or four percent."

Fed Governor Lawrence Lindsey, who leaves the organisation on February 5, has expressed reservations about inflation targets. He recently voiced concerns that such targets, similar to formal rules for monetary policy, could limit central bank flexibility.
Advocates say that if the Fed were to establish targets -- and meet them successfully -- the result could be not only lower inflation but a better performing U.S. economy.
They argue that achieving the goals would boost the Fed's credibility on inflation. That would reassure investors and reduce long-term interest rates, which in turn would help growth.

"It would provide certainty about policy so that investors and individuals can plan better," said former Cleveland Fed president Lee Hoskins, now the chief executive of Huntington Banchares. "It takes the risk premium out of interest rates."
Hoskins favours a law that would require the Fed to set multi-year inflation targets and provide for penalties if the goals are not achieved, as is the case in New Zealand.
FED MANDATE MIGHT HAVE TO CHANGE

Within the Fed, San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry has backed McDonough's general suggestion on an inflation range but said he might prefer a slightly narrower target of 0.5 percent to 1.5 percent.
Still, support for the targets is not unanimous. Even if it were, there are the problems with the CPI and adopting inflation targets might require a change in legislation.
The Humphrey-Hawkins Act mandates that the Fed pursue the dual goal of fighting inflation and promoting full employment.
Many experts said that setting a specific goal related to inflation might be at odds with that mandate.

"There isn't room for a formal inflation target right now. It couldn't be something written down in the Fed's procedures," said Roger Kubarych, a former New York Fed economist who is now general manager at Henry Kaufman and Co, who saw both pros and cons to the idea of inflation targets.
Parry said a change in legislation might not be required for the Fed to adopt inflation targets -- "as long as that is an objective that is generally acceptable to the population."

However, referring to legislation proposed by Florida Senator Connie Mack that would replace the dual Fed mandate with the sole goal of fighting inflation, Parry added: "It would help to have something like the Mack bill."
